A_target.statement:
Let $\map P t$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|property]] of finite [[Definition:Binary Tree|binary trees]].
Suppose $\map P {\mathsf {leaf} }$ holds and:
:$\forall l, r: \map P l \land \map P r \implies \map P {\map {\mathsf {node} } {l, r} }$
Then $\map P t$ holds for every finite binary tree $t$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\map P n$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|propositional function]] on $\N$.
Suppose $\map P 0$ holds and $\forall n: \map P n \implies \map P {n + 1}$.
Then $\map P n$ holds for all $n \in \N$.

derived.induction hypothesis on n: induction hypotheses on both l and r

object_map.reformulation: Generalize the single-predecessor step to a step ranging over all immediate substructures (here two), i.e. structural induction over an inductive type with a branching constructor.

validity_conditions: Finite binary trees are freely generated by {leaf, node}, so structural induction is valid.
Unlike the natural-number case, the step constructor has two recursive arguments, so the induction hypothesis must be assumed for both subtrees.
This branching is why it is plan-transfer, not a rename: the skeleton generalizes rather than matching one-to-one.
proof_plan: The constructors of $\N$ are $0$ and [[Definition:Successor Mapping|successor]]; those of binary trees are $\mathsf {leaf}$ and $\mathsf {node}$.

Map the base case $0$ to $\mathsf {leaf}$.
Map the single-predecessor step to a step assuming $P$ on each of the two subtrees.

The base-plus-step skeleton is reused, now with two induction hypotheses in the step.
Equivalently, apply the [[Second Principle of Mathematical Induction|strong induction]] on the number of nodes, since both subtrees are strictly smaller.

Hence tree induction is natural number induction generalized to a branching constructor, an instance of [[Principle of Structural Induction|structural induction]].
{{qed}}
